panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Patient 4 at 8y with classical GAN, axial FLAIR shows cerebellar hemisphere hyperintense lesion as captioned. B: Patient 4 at 8y with classical GAN, axial FLAIR part of A-C showing cerebellar hemisphere lesions. C: Patient 4 at 8y with classical GAN, axial FLAIR shows periventricular white matter high-intensity lesions. D: Patient 5 at 9y with classical GAN shows mild hyperintense lesion in periaqueductal gray matter of midbrain, which has no matching finding_key in vocabulary, so excluded per findings rule. E: Patient 5 at 14y with classical GAN, axial FLAIR shows expanded hyperintense lesions to bilateral cerebellar hemispheres. F: Patient 5 at 9y abdominal radiograph shows scoliosis and bowel gas accumulation, which have no matching finding_key in vocabulary (no scoliosis term, only pes cavus), so excluded per findings rule.

panels.figure_caption: Brain MRI and spinal imaging of Patients 4 and 5 with classical GAN. A–C Axial FLAIR images of Patient 4 at 8 years old revealing high-intensity lesions in the periventricular white matter and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, along with brainstem atrophy. D–E Axial FLAIR images of Patient 5 at 9 (D) and 14 years old (E). At 9, only a mild hyperintense lesion was observed in the periaqueductal gray matter of the midbrain. By 14 years of age, hyperintense lesions had expanded to the bilateral cerebellar hemispheres. F Abdominal radiograph of Patient 5 at 9 years old revealing scoliosis and bowel gas accumulation. FLAIR, fluid-attenuated inversion recovery

falls (> 10/day) by 9 years old led to medical evaluation. Physical examination revealed thick hair, macrocephaly, a high-arched palate, a saddle nose, enlarged tonsils, scoliosis, and obesity (Fig. 2F). Although dizziness and gaze-evoked nystagmus were present, cerebellar ataxia was absent. Upper-limb strength was normal, whereas lower-limb strength was significantly reduced (MMT 3), affecting distal flexors and causing foot drop.
